subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief statement which I am sure will be of interest to the Members of the House. As the House is aware, the automotive plan is designed to achieve a substantial expansion in production and employment in Canada and to promote improved efficiency in the automotive industries. Under the plan production in Canada will increase by several hundred million dollars annually and employment in the industry will grow accordingly. In this regard, during the year in which the previous automotive plan was in effect employment in the automotive industries increased by nearly 10,000 workers. Under the current plan the motor vehicle manufacturers and many parts manufacturers have already announced major expansion plans.
Organized labour and the automobile and automobile parts industries have welcomed the plan as a bold and constructive measure which is in the national interest. A major economic expansion of this nature, however, is bound to result in certain transitional adjustments for some workers and firms. In such cases there may be a temporary lay-off of workers while the company re-equips. There will be instances where firms will find it necessary to expand or re-equip their facilities to produce in greater volume and in the most efficient manner.
While such adjustments will take place in the context of very substantial growth in the industry, the Government believes that assistance should be provided to those who may be affected by the adjustment process in order to ease possible interim adverse effects. As a result the Government proposes to implement a program of transitional adjustment assistance for workers and firms in the automotive products industries. My colleague the Minister of Labour immediately following will be outlining the measures which the Government proposes to implement for workers in this industry. I would like to outline the program of adjustment assistance for firms.
The automotive plan offers new opportunities to Canadian automotive parts manufacturers for expanded production, rationalization of output and reduced costs. If Canadian parts makers are to take advantage of the plan, they must be increasingly competitive and flexible in their operations. In some instances they will be asked by their customers to make new products or to manufacture existing components on an expanded scale and more efficiently. As a result many Canadian parts makers will have to engage in substantial re-equipment and expansion programs to take advantage of the opportunities provided by the plan. In addition, increased working capital will be required in order to operate at expanded levels.
The Government wishes to ensure that every automotive products manufacturer who is energetic and shows initiative will have the opportunity to participate in the plan and is not prevented from doing so by an inability to acquire sufficient capital to accomplish
2908	COMMONS
Assistance to Auto Workers these objectives. As a result the Government is proposing to make loans available to those automotive products producers who have a reasonable prospect of profitable operation but who otherwise would be prevented from doing so through lack of financing. These loans will be made for the purpose of acquisition, construction, installation, modernization, development, conversion, or expansion of land, building, equipment, facilities or machinery and for use as working capital. They will carry an interest rate of 6 per cent and would be repayable over not more than 20 years for land and buildings and 10 years for other purposes.
A special fund will be set up for the purpose of making these loans, and the administration of this program will be the responsibility of an adjustment assistance board which is being set up specifically for this purpose. The Industrial Development Bank will be cooperating with the board and will be responsible for the day to day administration of the loans which are made under the program. Firms manufacturing the automotive products covered by the automotive plan will be eligible for the loans, except for companies which manufacture automobiles or firms affiliated with automobile manufactures.
The Government feels that this transitional assistance program for firms in the automotive products industry will make a real contribution to assisting firms, especially the smaller ones, to adjust to and take advantage of the many opportunities for expansion and efficiency provided by the automotive plan.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it would save the time of the House if my colleague the Minister of Labour could be heard on the complementary labour aspects of this program before general comments are offered.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. Member for Danforth and the House Leader for the Conservative Opposition that these two announce-
June 28. 1965	COMMONS
ments should have been made together because they are interrelated.
The announcement which has just been made concerns a most important issue and is a statement of the policy of the Government as far as the automotive industry and the recent arrangements made with the United States are concerned. If in the first place the Government had been concerned with the consumers of automobiles instead of passing the benefits of this agreement over to the manufacturers of automobiles, we would have had a far different situation today.
Because the benefit of this agreement has gone to the manufacturers of automobiles the Government is now forced to come to the assistance of the automotive parts manufacturers to provide the capital they need to be able to expand. It seems to me that it is a principle of enterprise that if you have a market for the product you are intending to manufacture there should not be any trouble in raising the money required in order to build your factory. But the approach of this Government has been a backward one from the very beginning, and they are now going backward again by way of taking Government money to provide for development of a parts manufacturing program.
What is wrong with our own Canadian investment dollar? Why cannot this money be found on the private market from people with savings and through the credit facilities of the tremendous corporations who are concerned in each case? In this way they could get the money from the investment and savings of Canadian people without requiring the Government to provide this capital.
It seems to me that the mistake made in policy in the first instance is now being repeated in order to give the manufacturers of automotive spare parts the same advantage that was given to automobile manufacturers. This is a complete mistake of policy, and is the kind of thing that is pushing us further and further into the situation where Government capital has to be provided to facilitate the expansion of our own industries. We are not just assisting the slide of the country into Government or state control; we are galloping headlong into it.
For those reasons I think this is a complete mistake of policy, and a case of one wrong perpetuating another. I regret that the Government has put itself into the position where it has to adopt this policy in order to protect the automotive parts manufacturers.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing a rather strange paradox in this country: the Canadian government borrows more and more, and thereby lends more and more. It is a strange paradox to see a government find ways to lend money while it is deep in debt. Why? Because laws have been passed to foster the growth of the Canadian automobile industry and it has become obvious that such laws were passed hastily and without sufficient study; new laws now have to be passed in an attempt to rescue certain related sectors which were affected by the previous legislation.
In a word, what we have are specialists and experts in certain fields who suggest the government pass laws which can be good for some areas, but which can create difficulties for other areas of the Canadian economy.
That is exactly what we have today. There has been too great a desire to help big companies. Perhaps debts had been incurred with the big automobile corporations. They were assisted and we are now faced with a deplorable situation, which arises from the fact that the government, with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in the lead, has not yet understood the real problem facing our present economic system.
In my opinion there is too great a tendency to finance production and too little desire to put at the disposal of the consumer the necessary purchasing power to absorb production. As a result, people on both sides of the fence, whether producer or consumer, are forced to borrow. Now, as the government has already borrowed considerably there is hardly any capital available and, today, the government is obliged to lend once more to private enterprise. This means that on both sides, producer as well as consumer, the situation is once more deplorable. In fact, the producer has to borrow from the government to finance his production, while the consumer, that is the buyer, has to go to finance companies to borrow again and again, in order to pay for production that has already been financed by means of loans.
Are we not heading for a vicious circle? Producers are borrowing in order to produce and consumers are borrowing to buy products which borrowing helped to produce. This is obviously a vicious circle and we do not know how to get out of it.
I am saying to the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), who seems determined to take all kinds of steps to assist the various sec-
June 28< 1965

Assistance to Auto Workers tors of the economy, that there is but one solution to get the economy out of the crisis, to end unemployment and to help designated areas; that can only be done if the consumer has the money he needs to buy what is produced.
When the consumer buys the production without borrowing, he finances production itself without the government constantly having to make loans to the producer.
Let us see to it that the consumer has the necessary purchasing power because he will then be able to finance production without everybody getting into debt, that is the government, the producer and the consumer who needs the products.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Industry has stated, the major expansion that will result from the Canada-United States automotive agreement will greatly increase employment in Canada. This expansion will involve a considerable reorganization of production with some consequent lay-offs of workers. These workers should not be asked to bear the entire financial burden of their unemployment. Because the economy as a whole will benefit from the agreement, it is reasonable that the people of Canada and the automotive companies assist the workers in meeting their adjustment problems.
I wish to announce the details of the Government's transitional assistance benefit program, developed for such workers. This program will provide assistance benefits ranging from 62 per cent to 75 per cent of the worker's weekly pay depending on the number of his dependants, provided this benefit does not exceed 65 per cent of average weekly wages and salaries in the motor vehicle and motor vehicle parts industries, which currently amounts to close to $75.
The duration of benefit is based on the length of employment in the automotive and parts industries. It can be a maximum of a year and a half for workers completing training programs. To be eligible, a worker must have at least 30 weeks of employment in the last 52 weeks prior to lay-off, which will entitle him to four weeks of benefit, with an additional week of benefit for every week of employment in excess of 30 weeks up to 26 weeks of benefit. For workers with more than 52 weeks of employment, a week of benefit will be received for every two weeks of employment up to a maximum of 52 weeks of benefit. To qualify for transi-
[Mr. Gr6goire.l
tional assistance benefit or TAB payments, a worker must also be qualified to receive unemployment insurance benefits.
Some of the workers laid off in these industries would normally be eligible for supplementary unemployment benefits. SUB is a scheme of unemployment benefits provided for in the labour-management agreements of the major motor vehicle companies and in a few of the motor vehicle parts companies. Under the terms of SUB plans, SUB payments would not be made if the transitional benefit together with unemployment insurance equalled or exceeded 62 per cent of the worker's pay plus a maximum of $6 for dependants. In these instances, under the TAB plan, the companies would be relieved from paying SUB benefits to their workers. It is the Government's view, however, that the companies, which will be receiving direct financial benefits under the automotive agreement, should meet part of the financial burden of the lay-offs. Accordingly companies with SUB plans will be asked to contribute to the TAB fund an amount equivalent to what they would have been required to pay to workers eligible for SUB benefits.
The payment of TAB benefits to workers eligible for SUB is conditional on such payments into the TAB fund by those companies having SUB plans. This provision would not affect workers who are employed in companies with SUB pirns, but who themselves are not eligible for SUB. I am glad to educate hon. Members in trade union terminology. These workers would receive transitional assistance benefits according to their entitlement.
The determination of whether workers laid off in the industry are eligible for TAB will be made by the adjustment assistance board. Workers will be eligible if the board finds that a significant number or proportion of the workers of a firm or plant will be laid off for a period of at least 30 days and that the lay-off was caused by a termination or significant decrease of production or activity arising from the operation of the Canada-United States automotive agreement.
Parliamentary approval will be sought for this program through an item in the amount of $5 million included in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Labour.

If the Minister of Labour went to Washington to bring in this plan, he should have stayed at home. I recall that on May 11, when he spoke in
June 28. 1965

this House, he said that whatever programs are available for displaced workers in this country, they are equivalent to what is provided in the United States under similar circumstances. Evidently the Minister has swallowed himself, or tried to swallow himself, by making this trip to the United States. What does he come back with, or at least what does he propose for us? In the United States I understand the workers in this industry who are displaced as a result of this United States-Canada agreement will receive up to $102 per week during the period of time they are laid off. We are told now the workers here will receive 65 per cent of their average weekly wage and the benefit will not exceed that amount.
The SUB plans, Mr. Speaker, have been in existence throughout Canada in this industry, and far exceed 65 per cent of the total take home pay while workers are employed. This program is certainly going to bring down the benefits to workers who are laid off in comparison with what they would have received under the SUB plan. The Minister says that in some instances the industry must contribute the same amount to this new TAB plan, as he calls it, as they contribute to the SUB plan, yet benefits to the workers are going to be a great deal less.
I think this program is far from satisfactory for the workers who are to be laid off as a direct result of an agreement this Government has signed with the United States, and which is being continued at the expense of the Canadian workers.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important for us to realize, first of all, that we are establishing an important principle here, one which we have requested for a number of months; namely, that where workers suffer dislocation as a result of conditions beyond their control they should not be asked to bear the burden of it. I think we are accepting that principle in this proposal. It is important also to note that those of us on this side of the House who foresaw many of these difficulties some months ago were laughed at and somewhat downgraded by the Government. Time has proven that these dislocations do take place and some assistance is necessary.
Evidently this program will become known as the TAB plan. I think it is important for us to try to establish at some stage just who is going to pick up the tab for the TAB plan. An analysis of the statement made today makes it rather obvious that it is the Cana-

Assistance to Auto Workers dian worker who is going to pick up the major portion of the tab. The first joker in the plan is that the payments are subject to a ceiling of 65 per cent of the average wage of workers in the trade as a whole, so the worker is automatically placed at a disadvantage in that regard. There are supplementary benefits, Mr. Speaker, but with the joker of a 65 per cent upper limit the worker is already at a disadvantage, more particularly as it affects these benefits.
It is for this reason I think the Minister will have difficulty with the various labour unions. Benefits are only going to be paid to the workers in those industries who agree to contribute into the TAB plan the payments they would have made into the SUB plan. Having given over $50 million in tax benefits, we now want to go back to the industry and say "You must take part of your social responsibility for this, and we would like you to agree to make this payment into the fund."
It seems to me there is a danger here that this is going to be the joker in the plan which will enable some of these companies to escape their responsibility. Really, on analysis, it is nothing but a substitution of the supplementary unemployment benefits for the benefits under the Government plan, with a slightly larger benefit for those who are eligible.
There are some advantages to the plan, but there are grave disadvantages. The United States workers are still eligible for benefits up to 85 per cent, so we are still considerably below what they are receiving in the United States. I had hoped there would have been some mention of a mobility clause which would enable these people to move around, but the statement is absolutely devoid of any such reference.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, it seems that while we have accepted a principle, there are grave deficiencies in it which I think will make it unacceptable to most of the organized trade unions in this field. As I have said, having given $50 million to the companies we are now going to ask them to come back in and make these payments and assume some of the responsibility. Finally, we are still leaving the Canadian workers considerably behind in benefits received as compared with United States workers.

They will take employment in other sections of our economy, such as in the supermarkets and so on after ten o'clock, or they will become salesmen. In effect they will be taking jobs away from other people; therefore we will not be helping the economy to the extent that the Minister forecasts. It is a hoax, so far as I can see.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one can easily realize, in reading the second statement, that there is something wrong in this whole thing, as there is a glaring inconsistency between both.
In the first statement, on the first page, the Minister of Industry and Defence Production (Mr. Drury) says;

In such cases there may be a temporary lay-off of workers while the company re-equips. There will be instances where firms will find it necessary to expand or re-equip their facilities to produce in greater volume and in the most efficient manner.
In his statement the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) said the opposite. He said that the worker will benefit from those advantages on one condition, namely that he will be laid off for a period of at least 30 days and that the lay-off will cause a termination or a significant decrease of production or other activity arising from the operation of the agreement.
In one case it is a question of equipment conversion to increase production, but the Minister of Labour said the exact opposite when he stated:
When such layoffs are due to a stoppage or an important decrease in production.
The Minister of Labour had more vision than the Minister of Industry and Defence Production. He realized that the trade agreement on the automobile industry would not only fail to favour the production of automobile parts, but would cause a decrease in the production of such automobile parts in Canada. That is why he stated:
Provided such layoffs are due to a stoppage or an important decrease in production. In such cases only, will workers be helped by the Minister of Labour's new plan.
Now, if employees are laid-off under the circumstances mentioned by the Minister of Industry and Defence Production, in other words, if they are laid-off temporarily during equipment conversion they will not participate in the plan suggested by the Minister of Labour, because the latter refers "to layoffs caused by abandonment of, or a great decrease in, production".
There is contradiction, or else the intention is that neither of the plans will have any effect and that the workers will not be able to profit by them.
It is high time, nevertheless, that members of the Cabinet fall in agreement and take the same decisions instead of contradictory decisions such as we have seen today, in less than one hour, by two members of the same government and of the same Cabinet, two ministers who are supposed to co-operate and who make contradictory statements.
One thing remains: according to the first statement, it is intended to allow the government to lend money to automobile producers, so that the latter may produce certain things which the consumers will have to borrow to buy. Since a loan has already been obtained
June 28, 1965

to manufacture those things another loan will have to be obtained to buy them.
On the other hand, the Minister of Labour intends to set up a benefit system for workers who are laid off because there is no more work for them since foreign producers have been allowed to invade and take over the domestic market.
Who will profit? The consumer? No, he pays the very same price for his car. Then who? Large automobile producers who are subsidiaries of American corporations while small Canadian producers of automotive parts will have their production cut off because of the agreements passed.
I think it is high time for this government to revise its position and instead of taking off tariff and taxes for large corporations only, they should take them off for all Canadian consumers and see to it that Canadian consumers have a sufficient and necessary purchasing power to buy Canadian automobiles and then our problems will be settled.
Let us stop administering and governing in terms of large foreign capital interests in most cases, or in terms of large finance corporations who will happily finance automobiles; let us legislate for the Canadian people by placing in their hands the purchasing power they need to buy automobiles without always going into debt. That is the only solution to the problem now facing us and we hope that the government will take it into consideration.

speechtext: Is the government now giving consideration to the proposal of the Canadian Association of Physicists made in 1956 and 1957, that Canada construct a high energy nuclear physics laboratory centred on a high energy particle accelerator, in Canada and, if not, what were the reasons for refusing this proposal of the Canadian Association of Physicists?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF HIGH ENERGY NUCLEAR PHYSICS LABORATORY
speechtext:
Subsequent to the brief submitted by the Canadian Association of Physicists to the chairman of the Committee of the Privy Council on Scientific and Industrial Research in October 1958, the National Research Council has not been aware of any specific proposal for the construction of a high energy nuclear physics laboratory. In so far as the National Research Council is concerned, there is no present plan to implement the brief of the Canadian Association of Physicists. Although the desirability of giving maximum possible support to physics is recognized, obligations to support other branches of science must also be taken into account. With the rapid expansion of universities and a plan for corresponding rapid expansion in the Council's program for scholarships and grants in aid of research in the next few years, it

is not considered possible at the present time to embark on a project of such magnitude. General support of physics in various fields in universities across the country including support for several medium energy laboratories is considered to be the most desirable way of utilizing available resources.

subtopic: U.S. FUNDS OBTAINED BY CANADIAN BANKS
U.S. FUNDS OBTAINED BY CANADIAN BANKS
speechtext:
1.	Does Canada exercise any control over American funds which are obtained on the market by New York agencies of Canadian banks, and, if so, by what means?
2.	Does either the Dominion Bureau of Statistics or the Bank of Canada maintain records relating to such transactions?
3.	Has any study been undertaken to ascertain the effects of these transactions upon Canada or upon international money markets?
4.	Has any study been undertaken to determine Canada's role in the Euro-dollar market?

speakeroldname: Mr. L. T. Pennell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: U.S. FUNDS OBTAINED BY CANADIAN BANKS
speechtext:
1. Canada does not exercise specific control over the operation of Canadian banks' New York agencies, but these agencies like any other branches of Canadian banks must comply with the provisions of the Bank Act. Under section 63 of the Bank Act, the Inspector General of Banks is required to satisfy himself that the financial condition of each bank is sound, and under the provisions of section 71(4) each bank is required to maintain adequate reserves against liabilities payable in foreign currencies.
In February this year guidelines were issued to all U.S. banks by the U.S. government as part of its program to improve the U.S. balance of payments position. In order to provide assurance that the foreign currency operations of our banks would not be inconsistent with these objectives, the Canadian government has requested all chartered banks to conduct their foreign currency operations
June 28. 1965

in such a way that the net position of their head offices and Canadian branches vis-a-vis residents of the United States is not reduced below the position which existed on December 31, 1964.
2.	Separate statistics on New York agencies are not maintained by the government or the Bank of Canada. However, over-all statistics of the operations of Canadian banks in foreign currencies have been maintained over many years. More detail statistics have been collected over the last two years.
3.	Changes in the statistics of our banks' position in foreign currencies are continually under review by the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada.
4.	The statistics mentioned in 3 above include information on the Euro-dollar market. No formal study has been prepared by Canada but Canadian representatives have participated in international discussions concerning the Euro-dollar market.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Industry which is of interest to quite a number of organizations in western Canada. June 28, 1965

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTIVITIES OF AREA DEVELOPMENT AGENCY
speechtext: Order paper.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTIVITIES OF AREA DEVELOPMENT AGENCY
speechtext: Surely this is a good type of question for the order paper. However, in view of the fact that there may be a short delay, if the Minister is prepared to answer perhaps it might be useful to clear the question.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTIVITIES OF AREA DEVELOPMENT AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will clear the question. There are six representatives of the Area Development Agency employed in the manner outlined in the hon. gentleman's question. The type of organization recommended varies with the size of the town or city, but generally it is suggested that each community form an independent industrial commission composed of representatives from the city or town council and the local Board of Trade or Chamber of Commerce, as the case may be, for the purpose of fostering the development of industry within the community.
If warranted, a recommendation may be made that the community consider hiring of a part time or full time industrial commissioner who can take the lead in carrying out industrial development work. In addition, in co-operation with provincial authorities the officers of the Area Development Agency have also indicated guide lines which interested communities might follow in outlining to industry the basic facilities and services which are available within an area.
In the case of the Province from which the hon. Member comes, in particular, the area development officer has been taking an extended tour through the main centres in the Province with the purpose of familiarizing himself with business and economic activities and also to advise these communities how they might best attract industries to their area. The tour has been arranged with the full knowledge and co-operation of the British Columbia Department of Industry and Commerce.

subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first take this somewhat belated opportunity of welcoming you back today from the functions in connection with the 700th anniversary of the first parliament, and the business meetings you had in Paris and Geneva, which we hope reached profitable conclusions.
Inquiries of the Ministry
My question today is to the Minister of Industry and possibly to the Minister of Justice. On four different occasions, the first being on May 11, I have requested information regarding the theft of 150 tons of cobalt contained in some 245 barrels or drums. I think it was on June 15, the day of my last question that the Minister of Industry said he would have a statement the following day. We are still waiting for some information about this preposterous situation, where strategic material was taken in such quantity and we cannot get any information about it.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think, as the House will be aware, that the cobalt in question was ordered at a time when cobalt was considered a strategic material to be stockpiled. Since then, however, the production of cobalt throughout the world has reached a point where it is no longer considered a strategic material-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext: It is stealable now, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext: -any more than would be nickel, chromium, tungsten or molybdenum. The 150 tons in question was in the custody of the producer and refiner of cobalt. It has disappeared from their premises. The Ontario Provincial Police have been assiduously undertaking an investigation of this theft. The Government has indicated to the company that it holds it responsible for the return of the cobalt, and we are now awaiting the results of the investigation by the Ontario Provincial Police.

subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is an intriguing question and I cannot interpret from the Minister's answer whether, strategic or not, this loss can be excused. On June 15 I asked who are the users of cobalt, locally or internationally, in so far as wanting such material in large quantity is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, without going into a lecture I might say that any industrialized nation is a substantial user of cobalt. This metal is used principally as an alloying element in many types of high speed steels, heat-resisting alloys and permanent magnet alloys. Dealing with the consumption of cobalt, I am told it is approximately 12,000 tons annually, and that this loss represents, as the hon. Member will understand, a very small fraction of the annual consumption of cobalt by industrialized nations.

subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext: What is its value?

subtopic: THEFT OF COBALT CONCENTRATE AT DELORO, ONT.
speechtext:
It involves some $100,000 of taxpayers' money.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. N. Thompson (Red Deer) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED PROTECTION AGAINST INTERFERENCE WITH PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to amending the provisions of the Expropriation Act (R.S.C. 1952, c. 106) with a view to giving greater protection to citizens against arbitrary interference with their property rights by departments of the federal government, and to the establishment of more suitable procedures for the transfer of title and possession of land expropriated under the authority of this Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to suggest to the House that it is urgent that consideration be given to amending the Act respecting the expropriation of lands. This year the free world celebrates the 750th anniversary of the signing of Magna Carta and the 700th anniversary of parliamentary government. Both of these historic occasions are reminders that freedom is indivisible, the freedom of one group must ultimately become the freedom of all. Recently the Archbishop of Canterbury said that Magna Carta was the act of one group, one order of the realm, asserting its own right; it was a cold, businesslike document, agreeing that certain political abuses must cease. I am convinced that the lesson of Magna Carta is as relevant today as it was in 1215 or at any time since.
The history of Parliament is the record of the resistance of the representatives of the people to the usurpation of powers by the Crown. I believe it would be foolish indeed to believe that, because we have a constitutional parliamentary government, we as the representatives of the people are not faced with the duty of keeping the powers of the Crown under control. In this spirit it has been brought forcibly to my attention to take a close look at the remarkable powers the Crown is at present given by statutes, in so far as the laws of expropriation are concerned.
It might be reasonable, Mr. Speaker, that in time of war and imminent danger to this country, the Federal Government should have such powers; but today such powers belong in

June 28, 1965
Expropriation Act
the War Measures Act, and not in any peacetime legislation. We already have far too much punitive federal law on our statute books. I am thinking particularly here of some of the provisions of the Income Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act, which may be justifiable during the time of national emergency but which are an open threat to the liberty and property of the citizen, now that war has been over for nearly 20 years. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the laws of this land, as they concern expropriation of private property were designed for a time of emergency, and certainly not for a time of peace such as we are living in at the moment.
As I interpret the Expropriation Act parliament has given officers of the civil service, down to the junior level, the right to deprive a citizen of the land which he owns merely by filing a plan in the registry office, leaving the citizen with nothing but the right to go to court to receive just payment for his land. There is no need to follow the usual provincial laws for the transfer of title. There is no need for a public hearing to ascertain whether or not any particular parcel of land is needed for public purposes. Powers like these contained in the Act relating to the expropriation of lands belong in a War Measures Act and certainly not in peacetime legislation.
Here in Ottawa many a home owner has awakened in the morning to read in the newspaper that his home has been included in expropriation plans of the day or the week before. I think, Mr. Speaker, that such should not be the case. I have in my files a number of letters and a number of briefs and submissions that have been made concerning the powers of expropriation which have been passed on by federal law to the National Capital Commission. Many of the citizens of this city feel there has been a flagrant abuse of the powers of expropriation. I should like to refer to the brief submitted to the National Capital Commission by the residents of the Rothwell Heights section, in the eastern section of the city. We read this:
We can understand that the Government should allow homes to be seized for a road, bridge, a school or some other essential purpose. We are totally unable to understand that the Government should allow homes to be wantonly destroyed to provide landscaped grounds for a suburban driveway.
Under present legislation, no citizen of Ottawa has firm title to his own land. Any day he may read in the newspaper, as we did, that following a secret decision of all-powerful officials, his home has been seized for some trivial reason without right of appeal.

I could go on to cite any number of cases which justify my contention that this Act should be rewritten. I do not have the time at my disposal this afternoon to give too many further illustrations that the powers of expropriation that are presently in the hands of the National Capital Commission are too broad. I could refer to the Silver Springs Farm, just west of town. From the records of the expropriation of this property, I do not see how anyone can believe that the rights of property ownership, which are basic in a democracy, are properly respected. These cases cover not only such property as Rothwell Heights and Silver Springs Farm but include any number of other properties here in the city.
Amongst the letters that have come to me in protest of these actions is one written by Mrs. Pilon, a woman in this city who does not have the power in her own hands to look after her rights. She says in a letter that she would like to tell me of her experience with the Federal District Commission, and I quote:
I know It is too late now for me to get any help but my experience might benefit someone else who is under expropriation.
A little over ten years ago my property which was approximately four acres was expropriated by the then F.D.C. It was situated on lot 27 Hare Avenue where the Putman Public School is now situated.
Then she goes on to tell of the ridiculously low price which was offered to her for the property; how she turned it down. Later, they offered her $7,500, and then they came back in further bargaining to offer $8,700. Finally, under protest at the continual pressure she was under she had to sell the property at an extremely low price without any attempt on the part of the National Capital Commission to protect her right to the property.
This goes much further than the National Capital Commission here, in Ottawa. The files of the courts, and I am sure many of the files of the departments, are filled with examples of how the Government, in peacetime and without warning, without having to say that this property was necessary for expropriation without returning to the rightful owner land that was expropriated once its use was no longer required, has expropriated lands. One particularly important case is the case of August Fontanna, a man living in Virden, Manitoba, who had his land expropriated for use as a federal airport during the war emergency.
June 28, 1965

June 28, 1965
Expropriation Act
tion, except in time of war, a public hearing should be held before a judge so that everyone can be satisfied that it is in the public interest for the land to be taken. No citizen, 1 believe, should ever be deprived of his property without at least having the privilege of his "day in court".
Likewise the exact method of expropriation should be spelled out in the act, such as the number of days notice to be given, with a safeguard that land would not be expropriated unnecessarily or by mistake, as has been done in past years.
I would suggest a clause be inserted elsewhere in the statutes of Canada guaranteeing a Canadian citizen the right to own property, and that this should be specifically quoted in the expropriation laws. We need that assurance.
I have looked over other sections of the Act which are important also. I believe far more trouble should be taken to assimilate federal expropriation procedure with the normal land title procedures of the respective provincial governments. Much confusion results from the fact that the filing of a plan can deprive a man of ownership of his land.
I notice that in section 7 of the Act there is no provision requiring the Government to expropriate the areas taken up by survey markers and national monuments that might be on or adjacent to such land, and such a provision should be inserted.
All one has to do is to ride around this city and the green belt area to see how many of these survey markers and monuments are left out of expropriated land, and which are now being defaced and destroyed. This is something that is not in the best interests of the public.
Another point which shows the complete inadequacy and foolishness of the act is concerned with section 16. This section deals with "any tenant in tail or for life, seigneur, guardian, tutor"-and a number of other people like lunatics, idiots, and married women-and I submit that the expression "married women" must be removed from that section. In a civilized society like we have in Canada we must assume married women are sane unless, like other human beings, they are declared otherwise.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
Section 22 deals with warrants for possession, and this section should include a paragraph which would outline all ethical, humane and honest legal steps that should

be taken before force is used. In my home community I have a neighbour, a man bom on a certain area of land. It belonged to his father before him. It had been passed on by his father to this man, his brother and mother. The land was required by the Department of National Defence and it was expropriated by the method I have outlined. It was taken from him, even though the title in Edmonton said he owned the land. The Government built communications towers on the land. I was astonished when, in January, 1964, I was called-

Thank you, I shall be brief. I thank all Members of the House. Anyway, I was called because this man needed help. When I reached this parcel of land I found that the Canadian Army had moved in. A whole truckload of soldiers were running across the fields in snow up to their waists, trying to catch the hogs, chickens and cattle which they were about to remove forcibly from the land, because this man had refused to submit to the expropriation order which, in this particular case, had come directly from Ottawa. I never dreamt that such a situation could arise in Canada. There are many complications attached to this case but I mention it as an example of the way in which a government or a department can use the tremendous power provided by the present legislation respecting expropriation.
I will close with a quotation from the Globe and Mail of June 14, 1965. The heading of this editorial is "Expropriation and injustice go hand in glove".
Government expropriation of private property is an unfortunate necessity in the planned development of municipalities, metropolitan areas and provincial districts. But the rules which govern expropriation should require that the needs of the property owner be weighed against the needs of the state. They should assure the property owner meticulously fair compensation and every assistance in making a convenient move. Government planners should tell property owners when their land is to be expropriated and they should tell them as soon as a decision is made. If an unconscionable time is to elapse between decision on expropriation and the actual takeover of the land, the owner should be repaid the losses he might suffer if the district stagnates while his property is in limbo. If he wishes to move at once the expropriating body should be required to accommodate him.
I think this article sums up most adequately what I have said. I believe it is not
June 28, 1965

good enough to expect a property owner, a man who may often not have much of this world's goods, to take up his case in the Exchequer Court, the only court of appeal open to him at this time. I know of only one case in Ottawa, despite the volume of N.C.C. proceedings, where this has been done, and in this case, having committed himself to costs of $28,000, the appellant had to withdraw.
This is not the kind of security that owners of property in this country should receive.
I wish the Government, in its zeal to make Canada a better country to live in, would take up this matter and bring in the necessary amendments to give us a proper expropriation authority, and I hope this can be done before the present session concludes.

speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) upon bringing this matter before the House. Those who have been around this chamber as long as I have-and I do not see any at the present time-will recall that this particular grievance has been mine since 1947 or 1948. I continued year after year, to call on the government of the day to give us a new Expropriation Act which would deal more fairly with the rights of citizens.
Perhaps I may be allowed to refer to a few previous speeches so that Members may know that on many occasions I have objected to the present method of expropriation. For example, in 1955 as recorded in Hansard at page 6910, I urged the Government to consider doing something about the method of acquiring land used by the Federal District Commission-it was the Federal District Commission in those days. At that time I said:
The use of the Expropriation Act in its present form is really not called for. I have always contended that the Expropriation Act was not meant to be used to acquire land of this type or under the circumstances in which the Federal District Commission is acquiring land at the present time. I realize it is a long time since I went to law school but I have always looked upon the Expropriation Act as being a violation of civil rights. I submit that it should be used sparingly by the Crown only in cases of great public interest, such as the acquisition of land for post offices, wharves, national defence buildings and so on. It should not be used too readily. If it is to be used as in the present case all advantages should devolve upon the party whose property is being expropriated. On behalf of those hundreds of people whose properties have been expropriated in the district here and who are voicing discontent over this procedure, may I say that I hope the government will see that this parliamentary committee to be set up next
Expropriation Act
session will make a complete study of the use of the Expropriation Act in acquiring land.
The time that elapses in the settlement of these cases is far too long.
It may surprise hon. Members to know that in some cases it takes as long as five years to reach a settlement.
In the following year, 1956, I said:
I shall only repeat what I have said on previous occasions, that I consider that the Expropriation Act, being an impingement upon the civil rights of a citizen, should be used lightly, sparingly but generously. Many of our people are not very happy. Hundreds of homes in this area have been expropriated by the Federal District Commission. There was no question of going to court. A private citizen cannot go to court against the government when an amount of $10,000 or $12,000 is involved, though big corporations or religious institutions can afford to do so because the amount involved is substantial. I have had very many complaints.
This is only to show that on many occasions in the past I was impelled to urge the government and the House to do something about the Expropriation Act. My sentiments go deeper. They are like those of the hon. Member for Red Deer, because I am one who is greatly in favour of the rights of private citizens, and particularly of the right to hold private property. I take special objection to that section of the Act which defines public work as being any work which the Minister decides is so. This is a relic of feudal days. There is no court or other body which has the power to decide whether or not the Minister has used his discretionary power correctly. As I said to my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Francis) a while ago, if the Minister were to decide that my chimney was a public work, it would be a public work and that is the end of it. All he has to do is to file a plan, serve notice, and the property belongs to the Government.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Therefore I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the first section which should be amended in the Expropriation Act is that which defines under what circumstances the property of a citizen of Canada may be expropriated. I believe that this section should be clearly defined. The Crown, in the year 1965 in any event, should not have the right to decide that it can expropriate anything at the whim of a Minister who has been advised by an official of a department of government.
Furthermore, when dealing with real property one must keep in mind that real property is a civil right which really is under the jurisdiction of the province. My contention

June 28, 1965
Expropriation Act
has been for all these years that in expropriating property for works which were not exactly or really for the use of the Crown in the right of Canada, the Government was impinging upon provincial rights. There are many circumstances, I claim, where if the Crown wants to expropriate property it should do so through the agency of the province or of the municipality.
There are now some cases, which I will not mention, before the Exchequer Court which deal with that particular angle. I feel, as I have always felt, that the right to expropriate by the Crown in the right of Canada should be limited to those public works which properly can be defined as works of the Dominion of Canada. I do not need to recall that some years ago this very argument was raised by a former Premier of Quebec, Mr. Maurice Duplessis, and I never heard that this contention was denied. There is, therefore, an area to be cleared up in the Expropriation Act, namely the definition of what is a public work.
I want it understood at this time, Mr. Speaker, that when I am speaking about the Expropriation Act I am not trying to attack the methods of expropriation taken by the N.C.C. or the Federal District Commission. After all, those bodies only carried on their duties with the assistance of an Act which was antiquated, and was the only means which the Government put at their disposal. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not want it to be taken that they could have done otherwise. They had to use the Expropriation Act as it stood. I blame successive governments for not having done anything about amending the Expropriation Act. Of course, there are real grievances with regard to the Expropriation Act besides the definition of what is a public work. There is the question of the method of settlement, the tender of an offer, the interest to be paid until settlement, and also the distribution of court costs.
Only a few years ago a former Minister of Justice, Hon. Donald Fleming, brought before the House an Act respecting the expropriation of land. That Act received first reading on October 3, 1962. There are very good suggested amendments to the present Expropriation Act contained in that bill. Certainly they should be incorporated in any bill which is to be brought before this House for consideration. Furthermore, I think the Government should take cognizance of the work done by the Ontario Commission which sat for about two years investigating the methods of

expropriation of land in Ontario. I do not know what has been done about this study. I hope the Government at the next session in the fall, or next year, will have produced a bill to be presented to this House which will incorporate some of the suggestions which have been made by the hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) and myself; but I would hope that at the same time such a bill would be sent to a committee for examination and discussion. Mr. Speaker, I want to give the opportunity to some other hon. Members to speak on this matter. I hope once again that this is the last time we will have to appeal to any government to produce a new Expropriation Act.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. Member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) I wish to congratulate the mover of this motion, which represents a principle that has concerned Members on all sides of this House. Looking back on the record I note that on October 3, 1962, the Minister of Justice at that time, Hon. Donald Fleming, introduced a bill which was then given the number C-50. It was described in his words as a "comprehensive measure relating to government expropriation. It will replace the present Expropriation Act. It is more than a mere codification or consolidation; it will introduce new provisions as well". That bill received first reading in this House, but unfortunately did not receive second or third readings; it did not become enacted into law.
The hon. Member for Essex East, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), also in 1962 introduced a private Member's bill dealing with this subject. I think it is quite clear that interest in the rectification of the present legislation extends to many quarters of this House, and indeed the views which have been so clearly and so well expounded by the mover of this motion are shared by many hon. Members.
The problem is not only one, as my colleague from Ottawa East pointed out, of the Federal Government; it is a problem which faces the provincial authorities and the municipal authorities. It is a power which is frequently given to many public bodies by their charter. I noted from the press, for example, and was a little shocked by this, the charges raised against my alma mater, the University of Toronto, in connection with an expropriation proceeding, where it was alleged that there was a conflict of interest in taking certain lands which were occupied, in contrast to certain lands which were unoccupied.
June 28, 1965

I do not quite know what the facts are, but when a question is raised it is quite clear that there is the possibility of injustice, and measures which would set out appropriate appeal procedures in connection with the decision, in the first instance, as to whether the property should or should not be taken should be spelled out in legislation.
In the particular constituency I have the honour to represent in this House a very large portion of the lands have been subject to expropriation procedures for green belt purposes. I am not quite sure what the order is, but it is of the order of 15 per cent of the entire land surplus of the riding I represent. It is a fairly substantial amount, and in dollar terms it is even more substantial. There have been many problems in this connection. I listened with a great deal of interest to some of the case histories which have been read into the record by the hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). The first name he mentioned is the name of a widow well known to myself. I was an alderman of the city council at the time of the events to which reference was made. I just want to say, Mr. Speaker, that in my own history of dealings with the National Capital Commission I think there is an effort to be fair. There is the procedure of a land committee. The land committee is a matter of public record. Any annual report of the National Capital Commission can be presented. They review every purchase, and have a procedure through which they use outside evaluators. These outside evaluators make records. The individual concerned can, if he wishes, hire an independent evaluator-appraiser and the results can be put together.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
In tendering for land, in the 1962 period there was a serious problem in Ottawa resulting from the rapid inflation of land prices. In the early 50's prices of the order of $1,200 per acre were a well substantiated figure in the area in which expropriation took place. Land prices rose very rapidly during this period and it was very difficult to be fair to the public and the individuals concerned. All I can say is that in my own experience the National Capital Commission has attempted, especially where a widow of modest means is involved in a situation like this, to be more than fair in dealing with such situation. Perfect justice is not meted out in this world in our courts or by the National Capital Commission or other bodies, but on balance I have had very few instances where the difficulties have been
Expropriation Act
such that I would be tempted to condemn public expropriation proceedings.
However, there have been some cases. The type of problem which I think should be given a good deal more attention than it presently receives in the development of expropriation policies under the green belt is that which involves a number of small businesses. I think in particular of the motel type of operation. A motel operation in the late 1950's could frequently be carried on the basis of cabins with a fairly small number of units and with a small dining room. This was a successful enterprise at that time. There are instances where expropriation has taken lands adjacent to and surrounding such a motel. This puts the motel in a situation where it cannot expand and the owner lives under a cloud of uncertainty as to whether or not he will be permitted to continue. There is no incentive to modernize and keep up with the times.
Frequently a small owner caught in this type of situation suffers a great deal. There are at least two or three instances of this nature which have been brought to my attention where I think there is the possibility that an injustice is being done. I say a possibility; I am not making any allegations in clear terms because the rights and wrongs and the full adding up of all the equities involved is a complicated business. But I think we should consider a procedure somewhat similar to that adopted in tax appeal cases.
I think that the legislation which was introduced in 1962 had a very desirable feature. It spelled out an interest rate of 5 per cent and then went on to provide that a tender must be made at the time of expropriation, interest running until the tender is submitted at double the rate. Therefore until the tender for the property was made interest would be payable at 10 per cent, which was a very strong incentive to the Crown agency involved to make a prompt tender in specific terms-which is surely the starting point for the rights of the party whose land has been expropriated. Another desirable feature which was very important was what I had in mind suggesting something like an income tax appeal board to which recourse by way of appeal could be had promptly and inexpensively. The problem in such cases is the expense involved. The party concerned may have substantial equities, but the equities are not in the form of liquid assets; they are in the form of property. A fairly valuable piece of property is involved amounting to a sizeable sum of money, but the owner of the property

June 28. 1965
Expropriation Act
does not have cash in the bank to hire the solicitors, the outside experts and the large number of technically trained persons necessary in this day and age to carry a fight on up to the Exchequer Court of Canada; and this imposes a strain on the resources of the party concerned which may constitute, in some instances, a denial of justice.
Surely a procedure should be evolved by which the cost could be more readily assumed, if we are to use courts as the test of these matters by the Crown. In this way the Crown could then say to the parties that this was the procedure by which their rights would be determined and the cost of such procedure would not be a deterrent to them in the exercise of this remedy. I think the procedure involved in income tax appeals is an eminently sound one. The costs are there, it is true, but the kind of decision which is made is usually a clear decision on the merits and it is arrived at reasonably promptly. This procedure has been evolved to deal with even more complex situations than are involved in expropriation of properties, and on the whole I think it has worked fairly successfully.
I should like to think that we could develop this principle in our legislation, spelling it out in more detail, such legislation, I would hope, being introduced by a Member representing the Government party in this House at some later date. I know that evidence of concern about property is clearly on the record, just as the concern expressed by my colleague from Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) a few minutes ago, a concern extending over some time, is one genuinely and sincerely held by him. It is also shared by many hon. Members on this side, including Members of the Government. But the development of legislation is not a simple matter. We on this side of the House have attempted to do many things in a relatively short period. This is one of the items, Mr. Speaker, on which I hope there will be further action at a later period.

That bill was the product of

considerable study by officials of the Department of Justice, and while it was introduced by the Minister of that day it was not called forth for further discussion by the Government of that day after its introduction.
Subsequent to the introduction of the bill the Department has received some comment on the terms of the proposed changes in the law. These have been and are being taken into consideration. Also since the introduction of the bill there have been a number of significant court decisions bearing on the existing law, and one decision in particular in the Supreme Court of Canada which has involved to a degree a new departure in the existing law, which has given law officers of the Crown reason to re-examine the bill introduced at that time to see whether through amendment the bill might be brought more into conformity with the law.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROTECTION AGAINST INTERFERENCE WITH PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not want to misconstrue what the hon. Member said; if I did misunderstand him let me hasten to correct it. However, I think the correction made by the hon. Member illustrates the proposition: that all hon. Members will agree on the absolutes of this problem. On the one hand there is the necessity for governments from time to time having to take, pursuant to the power of eminent domain, the use and occupation of land; and on the other hand, under the obligation of democratic governments, to act reasonably and fairly with regard to those citizens who may be adversely affected by such action.
The problem is really that of finding the appropriate procedure of administrative action to be taken in between. To some hon. Members who are familiar with some of the great issues in administrative law in past years, the famous English case of Crichel Down will be recalled, in which I believe the Minister of Agriculture had taken a certain portion of the farm for wartime purposes and had adamantly refused to reconvey it to the owner, even though the Crown no longer required it.
Essentially there are two problems here which hon. Members have touched upon but which, however, are distinct. First, several Members have touched upon the question of the reasonableness of a decision taken by an expropriating authority in taking the land itself. The policy of taking land must in essence have been decided by the Government itself, when it decided to carry forward a general plan of action. Presumably hon. Members will agree that this should be worked out by the Government itself as an incident of the general proposals which it is proposing to carry out. This question relates to the extent that the policy should be carried out, and whether or not two acres is enough or whether it should be five or seven; or whether the road, if it is to be a road, should be run through here or there, and to the question as to the extent that members of the public should be able to intervene and, by administrative action, try to show that the Government decision is unreasonable. That was the situation in the Crichel Down case and involves perhaps one of the most difficult questions in administrative law.
The bill introduced in this House in 1962 did not deal with that particular area of the question. It assumed the discretion on the part of any Minister of the Crown, acting in 22620-188
Expropriation Act
his proper sphere, to take land. The bill dealt with the second problem, namely the procedures and manner of the action to be followed when land is actually to be taken over, and it is in this connection that I think we can identify several objections which have been made by Members on various sides of the House as to the procedure which now exists in the law.
If I may, I perhaps can place them in this order. The requirement of notice; not only the putting of notice on the land title register, but also the requirement that some actual notice other than registration be given to the owner whose land is in fact being taken. You can imagine the number of people in a lifetime who would normally have their titles checked, or how many people in a lifetime would bother to go and see them personally, to look for an expropriation notice. The answer to that suggestion is, very few. I think this is not an unreasonable suggestion, that actual notice in writing should be given so that people will know that an issue has been raised in regard to the particular land and will thereby know exactly what the issue is. I would be glad to pass that suggestion on for consideration by the Government.
In this connection not only will the actual owners of the land be affected but also those who have some outstanding interest in the land, such as those who might benefit from right of way. They may have only the right to pass over the land. Perhaps notice should also be given to those individuals.
Second, there has also been a question raised as to the delay of compensation. As the hon. Member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) pointed out, an attempt has been made in the bill to impose punitive interest rates for any delay which takes place in respect of the land.
Third, there has been a question raised in respect of what happens after the initial use is exhausted, and whether, the Government having divested itself of the land, it should be returned to the former owner at cost. The suggestion here is that among those who should be entitled to compete for the land is the original owner, if he is still in the neighbourhood and still owns contiguous lands, and that he should have the privilege of bidding pre-emptively for the land, with the value of the resale price to be decided by arbitration.
The fourth problem is that which relates to the cost of proceedings. There is a certain level of interest in respect of a $100,000 piece

June 28, 1965
Expropriation Act
of property, and presumably the owner of the property will have no alternative but to litigate. However, in respect of a $5,000 or $7,000 piece of property-perhaps not very valuable by some individuals' standards but very valuable to a particular owner-this poses a very serious question relating to the possibility of incurring legal costs in excess of the actual return he will get from the property. The hon. Member for Carleton referred to the previous bill and the specific reference to the costs of these proceedings being paid by the Crown. Perhaps that might be the answer and that counsel acting on behalf of the Crown in appropriate cases should be allowed to pay costs of expropriation arbitrations.
The one thing I should like to make clear before taking my seat, however, has regard to a suggestion put forward by several hon. Members in relation to the ultimate right of the federal Government under expropriation law. This was referred to particularly by hon. Members in relation to the provisions of section 92(13) of the British North America Act, covering property and civil rights in the province. I think it is useful to mention to the House that under the provisions of section 92(10), while local works and undertakings-this is a phrase to be taken to include most real estate that might be expropriated-come under the jurisdiction of the provinces, by subsection (c) of that provision the federal Government is given power over such works, although as a whole situate within the province, as are declared to be in the interest of Canada as a whole. It is under that authority that the federal Government not only has the power to take the rights of a private citizen in land, but the rights of provincial governments themselves.
Mr. Speaker, hon. Members have made a number of valuable suggestions which I will take the opportunity to bring to the attention of the law officers of the Crown in their consideration of the Expropriation Bill.

Mr. Chairman, before six o'clock I had placed on the record the answers I received on behalf of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in respect of the De Luca matter, but there are certain questions which arise from those replies.
If De Luca, whose records were readily available to the Department of Immigration, was apprehended on March 17, why was it that it took until April 12 to determine that he had sufficient domicile in the country so as not to be subject to deportation proceedings? How is it that it took 25 days to make this determination, during which time he was confined to Bordeaux jail when, and this is
June 28, 1985

patently clear to me, the officials of that Department had this man's records before them, knew when he entered the country and knew the date on which he was apprehended? Domicile in this case is a statutory period of time; if a man has five years domicile he cannot be deported. However, he was detained for 25 days in order to ascertain this. Now, it is odd, too, that there were certain charges laid under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, but those charges were not founded so the man was not convicted. The other charges were withdrawn.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I think the Minister must answer as to why this was done. I am not trying to judge the man's character when I pose these questions. However, this man is a fairly recent arrival in this country, and has been here for five years. Under what right do we take him off the street, out of his job and incarcerate him for 25 days to establish that he has been in the country five years and therefore could not be the subject of deportation proceedings? I think we require a full explanation. The explanation so far is quite unacceptable under the circumstances. We do not think this should happen, because under the Criminal Code every man who is arrested has to appear in court and his case dealt with within a fixed period. A man cannot be detained indefinitely. When this does happen, certainly a rebuke is administered to the officials responsible. This is a travesty of justice when a man is detained improperly, whether under the Criminal Code or under the Immigration Act. It is still a violation of his rights and I must protest against this type of action. Certainly, the Minister must come forward with a better explanation than has appeared so far in this particular case.
Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to interrupt the hon. Member for Edmonton West, but for some minutes, we have not had a quorum in the House.

I have finished with that matter.
The other day the hon. Member for Ontario asked the Minister of National Revenue about certain administrative rulings that were being followed concerning certain products of the ice cream industry which hitherto had been free of federal sales tax. We have protests, naturally, from the Dairy Council of Canada and inquiries as to why this has happened. The other day the Minister did not give an answer, and I invite him to give us an answer now. This administrative ruling was made in 1950, and if it was made at that time certainly there was a justification for the ruling. However, 15 years later, we find a change. I know this has been done in the past in connection with various taxation matters, but there must be justification for the change. It is not merely a case of a quest for revenue. Therefore, I invite the Minister of National Revenue or his representative to tell us precisely why this is being done. Certainly it is not a case of idle speculation, because the Dairy Council has put out a number of inquiries in regard to it; so obviously it must be well founded.
This afternoon I asked the Minister of Finance a question as to whether or not there had been any protests, official or otherwise, from the United States Government with regard to the bank controls that were being imposed on the Mercantile Bank of Canada as a result of its ownership by the First National City Bank of New York. I do not know why this action was taken. We will be discussing the subject again in committee when the Bank Act is before the committee. I must confess I cannot understand why there should be an element of retroactivity. After all, the Mercantile Bank of Canada was never owned by Canadians. When it was incorporated in 1952, it was definitely all Dutch capital. Control by the First National City Bank of New York came into the picture when it first of all acquired a 50 per cent interest in this foreign owned bank. Subsequently it acquired the remaining 50 per cent. Now, for some reason a bank which has been operating in Canada for 13 years is told, you cannot expand because of this nationalism the Minister is trying to impose upon our banks.
I have before me an article written by that great pundit of Liberalism, Bruce Hutchison, who writes periodically from great heights in the Christian Science Monitor.
