I am dealing with the reply to the question this afternoon. I am sure the Minister has seen this type of comment. He may not have received official information from the United States Government, but I feel I must make this comment because the question is there. The Minister says he is going to deal with it at the appropriate time, perhaps in committee in October, November or perhaps in December when the committee has reported the legislation back to the House.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
However, this is not really the main burden of what I want to say tonight. This afternoon the hon. Member for Yukon raised the case of William Grant, a former Yukon Indian Agent at Whitehorse. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration indicated he had asked for a transcript of the judgment of Mr. Justice Parker. I trust he will read it because he will then see what I consider to be, not a prosecution but a persecution of a man whose record, according to the testimony of the trial and the editorials written since the verdict was handed down, was exemplary. This man was charged under six different counts with contraventions of the Financial Administration Act by making a false return to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
William Grant was suspended on May 15, 1963 after he had been transferred from the Yukon, according to what had been the undertaking given to him when he initially went there. He was a man of rather frail health who went up there in 1960. On account of his devotion to duty he decided against his own wishes and those of his wife to take on the job in the Yukon, but only for a limited time because his health would not stand it.
He was transferred south to Vernon in late 1962 or early 1963. Then his administration came under investigation and he was suspended in May 1963. But, Mr. Chairman, charges were not laid against him until November 5, 1964, after approval by the Minister of Justice. The charges were not laid by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration nor at his instance, because I think all will agree it is the decision of the Department of Justice and the Minister of Justice alone whether charges will be proceeded with or not.
This man went through his trial last week, and on Thursday Mr. Justice John Parker, even though over $70,000 was involved, fined him $10 on each charge, with one day in jail in the alternative. For the edification of hon. Members I will put on the record some of the things which were said by Mr. Justice Parker, and I hope that these words will sear the soul and brain of those people who were responsible for the charges in this case.
Mr. Justice Parker said:
It would be quite inappropriate to send Mr. Grant to jail. Suspended sentence doesn't really apply. It would be an insult to this man to say, "You will go free if you stay out of trouble'*... ridiculous. Mr. Grant is an exceptional man.
When it comes to a penalty, Grant's career was shattered.
In parenthesis I may say he has been operating a small grocery store and his wife is a matron of nursing in a neighbouring hospital in B.C.
He took certain risks, has said he was glad he did what he admits doing. He may still be glad, but he has suffered for it. There is no deterrent required ... how many public servants are going to take the risks Grant took to satisfy their conscience?
Mr. Grant could have sat and watched the people in his agency die...could have said I have only so much money to spend, this has to be, I've done what I can. He did not do this. He risked his career to do what he as a conscientious person on the spot thought he could do without bringing the Government down on him. It is largely a matter of luck whether or not a government official can achieve these things. My final comment on the morality of this case.. .1 like to think that had I been in Grant's position I would have had the courage to do as he did.
What was the offence? For housing some 2,500 people in the Yukon the department's allocation was $40,000, $16 per head on the average, and with respect to the conditions existing there one has only to read the evidence of the testimonials on behalf of Mr. Grant and the articles which appeared in the Western papers dealing with condi-

June 28, 1965

tions among the native population in the Yukon.
What did Grant do? As appeared in the evidence, like many another agent he had an almost open end cash relief account. He drew a cheque on it in favour of someone in the agency, as the need arose, and when the cheque was cashed the money was used to pay the accounts due. Some 70 houses were built and power lines installed. From the evidence it is clear that not one penny of this $70,000 found its way into Grant's pocket. As a matter of fact the evidence showed he paid money of his own in order to assist the native population.
Yet because of ambition, because of somebody's political decision, this man and an associate were brought before the courts. I shall read further from Justice Parker's judgment:
I doubt whether Indian Affairs ever got better value for expenditure than in those Mr. Grant made. Even the subsidizing of an Indian candidate for Sourdough Rendezvous Queen was a morale booster for the native people. Grant knew he could have got no authority to do what he felt was desirable there. He cleared the right of way, got poles for electrical power to Upper Liard. I believe him when he says he pointed this out to Commissioner Boys.
There is a real possibility of misunderstanding here. Commissioner Boys may have interpreted Mr. Grant's explanation as being a way of getting work out of Indians on relief payments.
Here is another interesting comment from the judgment:
It is interesting to note the Government of Canada has made no effort to recover any of the funds expended in this unauthorized way...the reason is perfectly clear. The Government is saying, in effect, "You had absolutely no right to do the things you did, but we quite agree with what you've done.
I read further from the judgment:
He had access to the parliamentary vote for Indian housing in the Yukon and Northern B.C.. . . a total of only about $40,000 per year. The cost of housing units was five or six thousand each.
So he knew he could do something to assist them to get better housing, though official funds were limited, there was no particular limit on the amount for relief funds at his disposal in Vote 519, designated for food, clothing, fuel and other relief objects.
I am satisfied Mr. Grant was aware of the practice in other agencies where cheques written on Vote 519 were used for other purposes as the Superintendent thought best. The number of needs here was higher than encountered elsewhere. So what he did was to write relief cheques payable to someone in the agency, have them endorsed and use the funds for housing and certain other purposes.
The pressures of conscience must have been very great...to anyone in the Yukon this makes very good sense...they would say, "Well, as a

taxpayer, I'm in favour of this." However, it was in absolute and direct violation of his instruction. He risked his career as a civil servant to do what his conscience told him should be done.
I now wish to quote from an editorial in the Edmonton Journal of Friday June 25:
Bureaucracy has seldom appeared more foolish or the law been made into a greater ass than in the outrageous prosecution of Mr. William Grant, the former Yukon Indian Agent.
In a trial before Mr. Justice Parker at Whitehorse Thursday, Mr. Grant was convicted of making false returns to the federal Indian Affairs Branch. . .
Mr. Justice Parker is to be highly commended on the sensible view he took of the case and for mitigating, so far as possible, the effects of the folly of the Indian Affairs Branch in prosecuting Mr. Grant.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
I would interpolate here that I do not think it is the folly of the Indian Affairs Branch. The prosecution was the direct decision of the Minister of Justice, and in passing I note that Mr. Grant has not been drawing any salary since May 15, 1963, and his associate has not been drawing any salary since September 1963. Yet we heard the Minister of Justice say the other day that a certain justice in Quebec who has been convicted of perjury who has appealed this conviction is continuing to draw his salary.
Shame.

Is this a case of there being one law for those high in office and another for those who are not so high? We are all equal, but I suppose some people are more equal than others, if I may poorly paraphrase George Orwell.

What did the hon.
Member for Lapointe say?
It is because he gave his place to the Minister of Justice, to run in his constituency.

Well, the hon. Member will make his own contribution. Those are his words.
This matter was suspended. Perhaps there was to be a cover-up. But why wait until November 5, 1964, to lay charges-18 months later? This is what we cannot understand.
I could tell you why.
Go ahead.

The Minister of National Revenue should listen to what this editorial has to say.
The judge said: 'T should like to think that had I been in Grant's position I would have had the courage to do as he did." But he added that Mr. Grant's actions had "shattered his career."

Why should his career be shattered? The Federal Government must make amends to a good and faithful servant-and very handsomely. Every Canadian with a sense of justice and fair play will demand nothing less.
Now I turn to an editorial in the Whitehorse Star of June 24, 1965:
When Mr. Justice John Parker delivered his masterful summation in Territorial Court Wednesday afternoon, only a handful of spectators was present. None of them remained unmoved by the tribute paid to Bill Grant, a little guy who broke the rules to do what he felt had to be done. There is general rejoicing throughout the Yukon today that justice was done in that courtroom.
Now that the long strain is over, and Bill Grant relaxes for the first time in two years (it has been that long since he was suspended by Indian Affairs) there are a few afterthoughts for the record.
No one can assess what it cost Grant and Armishaw to face trial on charges which were brought by some unknown person to the Crown... how can anguish and heartbreak be weighed? How can a child's sorrow and torment at the hands of others be measured? How is a value placed on a beloved mother who suffers a stroke because of a court case?
There is one economic yardstick which can be measured however.. .in dollars and cents, Bill Grant has lost at least $20,000 because of his actions on behalf of the Indians in the Yukon. He has lost two years' salary as Superintendent of Indian Agency, plus transportation and other incidental expenses to go back and forth to Whitehorse from his home in Vanderhoof, B.C. for arrainging, for preliminary hearing, for trial. Legal counsel is another expense item.
Bill Grant and Joe Armishaw were brought back under police escort, housed in the R.C.M.P. detachment jail like common criminals. They have been unable to find employment for the past two years with serious charges hanging over their heads.
As Judge Parker commented, no deterrent is required. .. how many civil servants would be willing to risk their careers as Grant did?
Is there no compensation aside from moral justification?
I have before me testimonials from a number of citizens of Whitehorse as to the manner in which this man worked for the Indians. They speak eloquently of his position in Whitehorse. I do not know Grant. I have had no contact with him. But the mere appearance of these things in black and white cries out for justice. We all know that in every department certain things are done-the rules are bent slightly; a way is found to do justice, to do the right thing. Parliament provides certain sums of money for use in the Indian Affairs Branch. Many a superintendent of Indian Affairs believes he should be developing a community of people who will not simply be waiting for cash handouts. Here, this money was used for housing. One only has to read the reports of the medical officer to visualize the state of housing for the native

people in Whitehorse-how unsanitary it was. But this was taken care of in part at least. And what was this man's recompense? A bureaucratic decision that he should be prosecuted. I say that this decision by the Department of Justice was a shabby decision, a shocking decision.
Now comes the question: What will happen to William Grant? Is he to bear the stigma of dismissal from Her Majesty's service because he was convicted on six charges under the Financial Administration Act, after he had put in 14 years of exemplary service? His service was valued service-
Would the hon. Member permit a question? Would he tell us who it was who provided the niggardly sums for housing to meet this situation?

This is the history all through. The situation is no better today than it was before. I am glad the hon. Member for York-Scarborough raised this point. It shows that all he can think of in this matter is partisan, political considerations. Nothing more is embodied in his question.
As always.

I am not excusing the
previous administration. I am saying that this situation is a blot on the conscience of us all. I am not excusing myself for only $40,000 being provided for the housing in that area. It was wrong. Let us admit it was wrong. But what I am talking about now is the man who tried to get away from that position, Parliament having voted other funds. No one has said we must recover the money. The cash relief provision could have been cut by 60 per cent and the money applied to housing. It was there. One hundred thousand dollars could have been available.

I feel we should have a full explanation why this man was prosecuted. Why was there this persistence in the prosecution? After all, the evidence is that many other agents had done similar things in the past-they, too, out of humanity. I am not suggesting that the end always justifies the means. But money has been provided and the department obviously knew what was happening. How could they possibly have been unaware, after

[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Also, the houses were going up; there were field inspections. This would be apparent. But somehow or other after Grant left the Yukon there was a complaint; and by whom? It would be interesting to know who made the complaint, and why. I wish to thank the Committee for the extended time, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might reply briefly to one of the points raised by the hon. Member who has just spoken. I refer to the De Luca case. I think I might suggest, having regard to the wording of the two answers to which my hon. friend referred, that it might be suspected that there was good reason for this. If a man has been tried in the courts and acquitted, one does not like to go into too much detail in answering a question.
I might, for the information of the hon. Member and others interested, state that in this particular case De Luca, within five years of his landing in Canada and before he had acquired domicile, was convicted of assaulting his wife and sentenced to a short term in jail; I believe it was some three days. He might have been deported at that time, technically, because he had committed a crime which warranted action under the Immigration Act; he had been convicted of an indictable offence before he had acquired domicile in this country.
Before he had acquired domicile, while he was in Italy on a visit, leaving his wife behind him with the young children referred to, the Immigration Department received information of a very disturbing nature from the wife. That information was referred to the police authorities promptly and an investigation was made. This was within a matter of days before the five years would have elapsed permitting this man to gain the status of a domiciled Canadian. He was picked up on an immigration warrant and charges were laid against him in the courts; serious charges were laid in the Family Court. The immigration authorities did not release him on bail because of the serious nature of the charges, and the Judge of the Family Court also refused bail in that particular case.
Before the immigration authorities had an opportunity to proceed with the hearing, which would have justified his deportation
Interim Supply
because he had been convicted, a prerogative writ was issued. Because of the prerogative writ they could not proceed with the immigration hearing, and he acquired the five years domicile while the prerogative writ was pending in the courts. I think he had been picked up during the third week of March and by early April he had acquired the five years domicile and the Immigration Department could take no further action.
But, Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend had wanted to see the file and the nature of the information, he had only to come to my office and he would have seen it. If he had done this I am quite sure he would not have been as critical of the Department as he has been today. The file is there and he can see it any time he wants to do so.

Mr. Chairman, why would the Minister tell me it takes 25 days to determine the fact that a man has acquired domicile? It is a simple case of mathematics. Whilst the Minister is considering his answer to that question perhaps he would address his mind to this point. Is it the practice of the Department to dredge out from maybe two years back a minor assault charge? I think one would have to really scrape the bottom of the barrel to justify deportation on that count and suggest that they are sufficient grounds.
This is the point that worries me. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I hold no brief for De Luca, but I am concerned with the time that was taken before he was released. If the release of April 12 was under the Family Court proceedings, then the Minister need only tell us that. I am concerned with how long the immigration authorities had him under detention.

He was released on April 12, Mr. Chairman. He was picked up on March 17. There were three charges laid under the Family Court Act, but in the meantime a prerogative writ was issued. My hon. friend knows that the hearing of a prerogative writ is within the jurisdiction of the court and not the Immigration Department, and we cannot proceed with an immigration hearing unless the ruling of the court permits us so to do. But before that prerogative writ issue had been disposed of he had acquired five years domicile in this country and we could take no further action. I wish my hon. friend would just take the time to come into my office and see the material that prompted the action in this case.

Mr. Chairman, there are two matters I would like to raise in this interim supply debate. I regret having to raise the first one but I do so because the matter has been raised time after time by other Members as well as myself and no action has been taken. So far as I am concerned, I am going to get up on every available opportunity until an injustice is corrected. The injustice is that the federal Government, quite legally but actually, is stealing some $1,500 a year from certain skilled tradesmen in their employ. I have never been able to understand why there is one policy in one department and an entirely different policy in another.
In the case of a skilled tradesman such as an electrician employed by the Department of Public Works in this building, he receives what is known as the prevailing rate. An electrician employed by the Department of Public Works has to have the same knowledge and does the same work as the electrician who works for a private contractor outside the public service. This is an accepted principle, and has been for years and years, in the Department of Public Works. But when we come to an electrician employed by the Department of National Defence in the dockyard at Esquimau, then the prevailing rate structure does not apply.
I have raised this matter before and, as I say, I am raising it now and am going to keep on raising it until the situation is corrected. I will admit that I have a particular interest in this question because by trade I am an electrician myself and I know what these men are up against. There is only one difference between the electricians in the dockyard and myself, and that is that although I am trained to give light the same as they are, I also try to give light in a different way in this House of Commons.
An electrician in the dockyard at Esquimau never goes on board ship-that is, the inside wireman-and therefore never does any work on board ship. Therefore he is not a marine electrician. Yet the Government insists on classifying the electricians in the dockyard at Esquimau who never go on board ship, who have to do all the work that any other electrician has to do and have to have all the qualifications, as marine electricians and not as inside wiremen. This is the way they are classified by the department. A marine electrician receives $3.05 an hour; that is the prevailing rate. But an inside wireman in Victoria receives $3.85 an hour as the prevailing rate.

[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
Year after year this department refuses to recognize that they are inside wiremen and they are not marine electricians, and because of this outright discrimination they are stealing $1,500 a year from the electricians employed by the Department of National Defence in the dockyard at Esquimau. These inside wiremen not only do maintenance work but they have to do construction work. They have to handle pumps and other electric motors with ratings as high as 2,300 volts which marine electricians are not qualified or allowed to handle. Yet we have a continuation of this situation.
The situation is even worse for the linemen working in the dockyard. These linemen handle hot, as it is called. They handle up to 60,000 volts. They handle hot anything, from 110 volts, 220-240 volts, 2,300-2,400 right up to 60,000 volts. The B.C. hydro men outside the camps are paid $3.42 an hour. The linemen inside the fence working for the Government are paid $2.95 an hour, instead of $3.42. I say this is absolutely unfair and is against what has always been the policy in most Government departments, namely that skilled workmen, be they electricians, carpenters, painters, plumbers or steamfit-ters are paid the prevailing rate; and the prevailing rate is the union rate. In Victoria the Department of National Defence furthers this injustice by stealing from qualified workmen $1,500 a year by way of salary. I hope that this will be the last time that I, the hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich and others have to draw this discrimination to the attention of the Government. Before the House meets following the recess, which I understand is going to come about, I hope that corrective action will be taken in the payment of union wages to federal employees who are entitled to them, and that some consideration will be given to making this payment retroactive for at least a reasonable period of time.
There is one other matter I want to raise on interim supply, which provides the only occasion on which I can raise it. The City of Vancouver is not only a major port of Canada, but it is one of the major exporting ports of the world. There is a labour dispute taking place in the City of Vancouver. One of the elevators has been closed for a period of time. The union workers in Vancouver have, however, played fair with the farmers of this country and with the port of Vancouver and the Government in that, out-
June 28, 1965

side of this one elevator, all other elevators have been kept in operation and these men are prepared to move the wheat from the elevators to the ships just as fast as the ships come into port and the wheat becomes available.
However, Mr. Chairman, what is happening is this. The other elevator companies are by their actions blacklisting the port of Vancouver. They are by their actions being unfair to the farmers and laying the foundation for antagonism of the unions so that the strike will spread. Only yesterday I believe the Minister of Labour received a telegram from the United Brewery, Flour, Cereal, Soft Drink and Distillery Workers of America. This is the union concerned in the present dispute in Vancouver. I think that this matter is of such importance that the only way that we can assure a sense of decency on the part of these firms to their employees, the farmers of Canada and the Government is to place on record the complaint which has been officially brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour. Therefore having received a copy from the employees of the union concerned I should like to read this telegram. It reads as follows:
Having promised the government to try and keep the export grain flowing through port of Vancouver by not spreading the strike to other elevators, while current industrial commission attempting settlement, unless provoked into doing so, the union urgently requests you to cause an investigation as to:	(a) why are so many ships lying in the stream
during the past six weeks, waiting to receive grain cargoes;
(b)	why the operating elevators do not and have not had the proper grades, e.g. Durum wheat, etc. on hand in sufficient quantity and why they have large vacant storage space at present;
(c)	why railroad cars from the prairie were reduced to a trickle on one or more occasions during last two months;
(d)	why many grain berths and loading spout facilities at operating elevators have been vacant and out of use during the past several weeks;
(e)	why one large elevator is cutting off receiving cars from three to five days so it can conduct a weighover, i.e. a Government inspection of grain on hand, when ships are waiting for wheat and prairie farmers are waiting to ship. Surely an extension could have been given this elevator by the board to protect its licence, if this is the problem;
(f)	why in light of above, farmers at east-west shipping point in Saskatchewan have not been able to have their storage grain shipped so as to clean out their bins for new crop;
(g)	why board developed new camouflage twist of placing on outside of cars cards designating other elevators as consignee yet when opened such cars have Alberta Wheat Pool grain tags inside.
This is the elevator that is being struck, Sir.

This causes a struck company's grain to go into an unstruck elevator. It is a provocative move to possibly expand strike. Although unsavoury the union is urging its members to handle this wheat in order not to fall victim of companies provocations to expand strike, at least during incumbency of Commission.
Copy of this wire sent to house leaders-
Etcetera. That telegram is signed by Mr. E. C. Sims on behalf of the grain workers union.
I do not apologize, Mr. Chairman, for taking up the time of this Committee in reading the telegram or raising this issue on interim supply. The farmers want to ship the wheat they have in stock, so as to clean their bins and be prepared for the new crop. The port of Vancouver wants to ship the grain. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is proud of the contracts he has been able to sign in connection with the export of Canadian wheat. The City of Vancouver wants the port kept open. The employees want to reach an amicable understanding with their employers. They do not want to close the port. They have shut down one elevator only as a demonstration of their demands and have left the others in operation. Yet the evidence from the union in Vancouver that the elevator companies are being provocative and are trying to provoke by their action the unions into expanding the strike, a strike which the Vancouver workers do not want, is conclusive. They are very definitely trying to provoke an expansion of the strike by placing labels on the outside of railway freight cars designating them for elevators which have not been struck. However, when the union men open the doors of those freight cars they find that they were originally intended for the Alberta wheat pool elevators which have been struck.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
I know that all Members of this House want to see wheat flowing through the port of Vancouver, and the way to ensure this is to refuse to be part or parcel of mislabelling of freight cars, and to make sure that every bit of storage in elevators in Vancouver which have not been struck is fully utilized.
According to the telegram to which I referred there were not less than six ships in mid-stream Vancouver harbour waiting to be loaded with wheat, which apparently the other elevators were not prepared to supply because of their attempt to create the impression that elevator employees and unions are the ones who are responsible for the expansion of any tie-up in the City of Vancouver.

I think 1 have said enough to emphasize not only the importance of this matter but to draw this situation to the attention of the Minister of Labour. I have done so with the hope that he will not receive this telegram without doing something about it. He has very capable employees in Vancouver and I feel that he should give them explicit instructions to see that elevators which have not been struck are operating at full capacity to the benefit of the workers, the City of Vancouver, the farmers and this country as a whole. I want to reiterate my hope that the Member for Esquimalt-Saanich and myself will not have to get up again to ask for decency and fair play for the employees in the dockyards at Esquimalt in order that they may obtain their rights to receive prevailing rates, because they are qualified and they have to do the work.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take up a few minutes to raise a question of interest to all C.N.R. station masters, from Vancouver to Newfoundland.
Some time ago, I received representations from C.N.R. station masters and got in touch immediately with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill). I should like to read a few paragraphs from my letter, so that all the members, and more particularly the government members, might know the injustice which is being done by C.N.R. officials to station masters who have worked for that company for 15, 20 and even 30 years. Now, this is what I wrote to the Minister of Transport on April 14, 1965:
Honourable Sir:
I am informed that the Canadian National Railways intend to take away from station agents the express commissions on the line from Vancouver to Newfoundland. It seems that this amount paid in addition to the station masters' salaries amounted to over one million dollars. As a compensation, the C.N.R. has offered approximately $300,000 to be distributed in lieu of commissions.
And there I mentioned to the Minister of Transport that a few station agents had asked me to intervene on their behalf to correct, if possible, the new policy which C.N.R. officials intended to adopt.
In addition, I pointed out in my letter that those persons told me that this compensation would represent approximately one fourth of the amount they received previously as commissions. This means that a station master who received $500 in commissions to do this work would only receive about $125 under this new policy.

On April 15, the minister acknowledged receipt of my letter and on June 10, he replied that he had received from the C.N.R. a report on my remarks about the proposed removal of the commissions. The authorities of the company also advised the Minister that the matter had been discussed with the Order of Railway Telegraphers for several years and that negotiations were under way with that organization.
The minister also suggested that those concerned be asked to submit the usual representations to their unions.
I want to point out this evening that station masters employed by the C.N.R. for many years got from $100 to $5,000 in commissions for their work. Those commissions cost a little over $1 million every year to the C.N.R. and now the company offers its station masters a compensation of $375,000, or approximately 25 per cent of the amount paid previously. In short, instead of getting a salary increase, as in every other segment of society, and in every other trade or profession, those C.N.R. employees must accept a rather substantial reduction.
I even met a station master who told me that this new policy would cost him over a thousand dollars a year in salary.
The company told the station masters to make their representations to their union, but the employees told us that the latter had informed them that they had to accept the company's offer because it seemed final.
At a meeting last May 13, the company offered station masters the sum of $250,000. According to a press release company officials stated:

-Company is desirous of withdrawing Express Commissions either through negotiations with us or by other means.

Mr. Chairman, that means that the station masters concerned had no other choice than to accept the company's offer, in order to obtain the largest amount possible, because the company would take other steps to withdraw express commissions.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
After drawn-out negotiations, the union concerned was forced to accept an amount of $375,000 which was distributed as follows: 6 per cent in the Atlantic provinces, 25 per cent in the St. Lawrence region, 24 per cent in the Great Lakes area, 24 per cent in the Prairies and 11 per cent among the station agents of the Mountain region. The station
June 28. 1965

agents will be forced to accept this amount and will have no other recourse. As a consequence, agents in my region as in others, will see their salaries reduced by $500, $800, $1,200 or $1,500 a year.
At present station agents are wondering if the C.P.R. has acted the same way. They would also like to know if this crown company, which receives federal grants, can actually reduce their earnings by eliminating the payment of commissions, and whether, in the next few months, the company will announce a salary revision so that they may receive as much money as they did prior to this agreement, to provide for their family's needs.
I take this opportunity to thank the minister, first for having answered my letter, and second, for having asked the C.N.R. for a report. I also wish to ask the minister to give this matter further study and to see if there has not been any discrimination against those C.N.R. station agents. It should also be determined whether those agents who, as I said earlier, received up to $4,000 in commissions but will henceforth be receiving only $1,000 to $1,500, will have their loss offset by an increase in salary of $2,000 to $2,500 a year.
I am sure that if the minister takes the trouble to study the question-and I know that he will do so-he will find that the people concerned have good grounds to fear the worst. Indeed, if members of all professions are getting salary raises at this time, it is inconceivable that this group of citizens, in all Canadian provinces, should suffer a salary decrease.
The second point I wish to make on interim supply arises from a certain statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays). We know that, at the present time, one must be very cautious in Canada as to the words one uses and the action one takes to achieve greater unity and understanding between western and eastern farmers. Sometimes, certain statements shock us and rightly so.
As far as I am concerned, as a citizen of eastern Canada and as a practising farmer, I do not want to criticize in any way western farmers or the present or the past governments for passing legislation in favour of farmers in the western provinces. What I want is that, instead of destroying the action taken in favour of western farmers by the governments, farmers from eastern Canada should find a way to profit by the advantages offered by the federal government. Too often in the past, there seemed to be attempts 22620-1891
Interim Supply
to rouse one group against the other, and in fact, we, in eastern Canada, have noticed, that such was, in a way, the policy of those who govern the affairs of this country.
Thus, during the last electoral campaigns, candidates in eastern cities, such as Toronto and Montreal, said that the Conservative party, when in office, favoured western Canada much too much. A feeling of distrust was created here against the Conservative party and western farmers who, it was said, were always asking the federal government for money under the crop insurance act and other legislation. It was even claimed that those statutes protected only western farmers. In my opinion, that campaign was disastrous for national unity and for eastern farmers.
I should like to make this appeal: Let us put an end to those suggestions and remarks which tend to divide rather than unite.
If every time a group, either from the east or the west, wants some legislation to be passed, another group objects thereto on the grounds that the government is doing too much for one part of the population, we are really going to divide Canada.
I should like to refer to what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) said last December-I was then recuperating from a car accident-before the Canadian federation of farmers at the Empress Hotel in British Columbia. I have read his remarks again and again, but it is the first time that I have the opportunity to quote them in the house for the information of all hon. Members and also for the edification of eastern farmers, so that they know exactly that the good old policy of the Liberal party of going into one part of the country to arouse its people against those of another area still prevails.
I will simply read without any comment what the Minister of Agriculture said. I am sure that everybody will be able to analyse his words and their purport.
I quote in English the minister's statement:
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

Achievements such as these have been due in large part to the capacity and ability of your farm people and leaders.
They have been due also, I would think, to the fact that there is still a pioneering spirit here, a willingness to try new approaches and break new ground.

This happened in British Columbia, Mr. Chairman.

As a matter of fact I sometimes wish we could transport some of this vigorous pioneering spirit,

June 28, 1965
Interim Supply
this eager open-mindedness and willingness to try new ideas which is so typical of the whole west -including the west I come from-to other parts of our country.
I know I'm prejudiced, but I think it would tone up some of our eastern provinces to have a little more of this healthy western pioneering spirit down there.

Mr. Chairman, I know that westerners are broadminded and willing to accept new ideas, new ways of dealing with problems, but it does not follow, as the Minister of Agriculture seemed to insinuate, that farmers of eastern Canada, Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes, are narrowminded and unwilling to consider new ideas. If the minister created that impression in western Canada about the Ontario, Quebec and Maritime farmers, I would invite my hon. friends from the western provinces and British Columbia to come to the east, to Ontario, to my own province of Quebec, or to the Maritimes where they will meet farmers who are not narrowminded but willing to accept new ideas to improve their lot and help their profession.
However, none of those new ideas should be along the lines once suggested by the Minister of Agriculture, namely that the Quebec farmer could live with the proceeds from six cows and two sows and that the Quebec members who spoke in the house of a recession in agriculture were talking through their hats. That is no way of introducing new ideas or of dealing with a segment of the population which wants to live on Canadian soil and participate in the achievements of our national economy.
Frequently, organizations or people draw our attention to statements made by the Minister of Agriculture. At first we hoped that the minister would check his bursts of temper, stop making wanton statements or think twice before making great statements.
Some time ago Ontario farmers organized by the Ontario farmers' union marched on the federal capital. They came to ask the federal government to consider their problems and find a solution so that farmers could get a decent income, which is only right. In fact, if, according to statistics, the average income of the whole family is $7,200 this year, the average income of the eastern farmers family is much lower than that. If the government wants farmer income to increase proportionately, it should cease to make improper remarks against farm organizations and farmers.
The Minister of Agriculture had this to say about this march:

The brief presented by the marchers contained "serious factual errors in statistics and glaring contradictions in its own policy statements." No government can be impressed by this sort of presentation, he added.

And the minister continued further on:

Before agitating for action, surely it should know exactly what action it is agitating for. It seems to me that any other approach is purely irresponsible. And I don't just think Canada can afford this kind of irresponsibility inside or outside our politics.

This means, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Agriculture was simply saying to these people that their brief concerning a certain policy was nonsense, irresponsible, and that the figures quoted were wrong; that these men who had taken the trouble to study data from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and the Department of Agriculture, these men who had come here to the federal capital to submit a true picture of farming in Ontario, were all wrong. They came here to ask that a specific policy be adopted, and they were told once more, and this to the Chamber of Commerce of Alberta, they had not considered the matter, in short, that they did not know what they were talking about. I suggest that such an answer tends to divide rather than unite the country or the classes of society, or the eastern and western farmers.
If the Minister of Agriculture has something to say to Ontario farmers, instead of doing so before the Chamber of Commerce of Alberta, he should have the courage to tell them face to face, or else in the course of a meeting in his office. If the Minister of Agriculture has something to say against the eastern farmers, let him not go to the Empress hotel, in British Columbia, and tell western farmers what is going on in eastern Canada; instead he should at least have the decency to reply to farmers of eastern Canada, to discuss with them the problems the East has to face and not go and discredit these people before their fellow citizens, counterparts or friends in western Canada. As far as we are concerned, we want others to succeed in their own region, but we also wish to succeed at home.
I shall conclude my remarks on these two points which I think, are significant; first, I hope the Minister of Transport will give

June 28, 1965

immediate attention to the station agents of the Canadian National Railways in my province and in the eastern provinces; second, I hope the Minister of Agriculture will once and for all put an end to those unpleasant remarks about eastern farmers when he speaks to western farmers.
For my part and as far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we shall never agree to criticize or campaign against the present government if it helps western farmers, but I want the same attitude to be adopted by the government when its ministers come and make political speeches in my province and in all eastern Canada.

speechtext:
I wish to make a few remarks on clause 1 with regard to the proposed amendments to this Act. Generally speaking we are in favour of the proposals. We think they are good, though they do not in all respects conform to the recommendations of the veterans organizations. I admit these organizations have approved the schedule of payments and income limits.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The first point at which I suggest the present amendments are amiss is the provision for maximum income allowable to a married couple. The maximum income allowed under the terms of the present bill has been increased to $220, and the allowance has been increased to $161 a month. I wish to take up the case of the married veteran who has dependants-veterans who were granted war veterans allowance under section 3(l)(c). That is the provision which allows a veteran to obtain war veterans allowance because of unemployability. 1 have on my records an example which I referred to the Minister, and under the existing legislation the Minister of course had no alternative but to deny the application. This was a young veteran of 35 years of age who under section 3(l)(c) of the War Veterans Allowance Act was declared to be unemployable because of a serious heart condition. He had five children. Under the
June 28, 1965

War Veterans Allowance Act existing legislation and under the proposed legislation the maximum that can be granted to him out of the assistance fund is the maximum income allowable under the War Veterans Allowance Act, which is now $221 a month.
I admit, of course, and recognize that any allowance this couple would receive under the Family Allowance Act and under provincial social legislation is not considered as income-that is, any other such income- for the purpose of the ceiling of the War Veterans Allowance Act. But the fact of the matter is that in certain provinces, and certainly in British Columbia, the ceiling established by the War Veterans Allowance Act is greater than the ceiling allowed by the provincial government for social assistance. The result is that we get a married couple, without any children, receiving $221 a month. We also have another married couple where the husband is also in receipt of war vet-terans allowance, with five children, who are allowed exactly the same amount and the same ceiling. What I am suggesting is that the Minister consider merely raising the ceiling of allowable income to those war veterans allowance recipients who have dependant children. It will not cost any more money under the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am suggesting that the Minister merely raise the ceiling by say $25 per month for each dependant child. Then under the assistance fund they could receive an additional allowance, and if they do not receive the additional allowance because the board will not grant it to them, at least the wife could go out and work. The husband himself is unemployable, he has been declared so by medical certificate. The wife could go out and earn more money to support the five children, or however many there may be.
I suggest to the Minister that the situation is so obviously inequitable that it warrants his serious consideration. I have suggested that the maximum allowable income be increased by say $25 a month for each dependant child. I would appeal to the Minister to do this. I know he is interested in this matter and I ask that he consider this proposal very seriously under the present bill.
We are anxious to get this legislation through. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, there is not the same anxiety to get the war veterans allowance amendments through tonight or tomorrow because the increases are already in effect. But there are other ways in which

this legislation could be improved. I could go on for some time describing some of the other inequities that exist under the War Veterans Allowance Act and which are not remedied by the proposed amendments. I would suggest to the Minister that perhaps this bill might be referred to the standing committee; but if it is not, let me mention another problem that has been brought to my attention on many, many occasions.
I realize this is somewhat of a departure from the original principle of war veterans allowance. One of the greatest difficulties I have seen with recipients of war veterans allowance concerns medical expenses incurred by the wife. I would suggest to the Minister that he seriously consider that the wife and also, of course, dependant children of a recipient be taken care of as far as treatment is concerned. Without going into any other anomalies that I have noticed, may I suggest to the Minister that if it cannot be done now, in the future the war veterans allowance be tied to an index, I would not say to the cost of living index but to the average standard of wages. It seems that veterans organizations are reasonably satisfied with the rate set under the proposed amendment and as established by the House last September. If this is a reasonable standard, let us tie it to the increase in wages of the people of the country. I think this would be very beneficial in the future, provided you use the right index, not the index used in the Canada Pension Plan, and escalate the war veterans allowance as the standard of wages across the country goes up.
May I again refer to the question of the increase in the allowable income to those recipients who have children. Remember, Mr. Chairman, that under the Canada Pension Plan an orphan is defined as being a child of a breadwinner who has died, and is given an allowance of $25 a month. This applies to each child up to four, and the allowance is $12.50 a month for each child thereafter. These people in receipt of war veterans allowance because of unemployability are not able to qualify their future orphans for this allowance.
Sometimes there is lack of consultation between one department and another. In this case I believe the Minister and his staff should consider the difference between the allowance in respect of an orphan where a recipient of war veterans allowance has died and should put the widow in the same category as a married veteran. But the chil-

June 28, 1965	COMMONS
dren of the deceased war veterans allowance recipient cannot qualify for the orphan's benefit which is given under the Canada Pension Plan. Therefore there is all the more reason, I suggest to the Minister in all sincerity, for his considering at the very least raising the maximum income allowable to a married couple with dependant children.

Mr. Chairman, I have one point to put before the Minister. It is one that I have raised on previous occasions and I have spoken to the Minister privately about this. It concerns Canadian servicemen who are abroad and have not come back to Canada since either the end of World War I or World War II. They would in all respects qualify for pension except with regard to the residence requirement of one year in Canada. If I remember rightly, this is one of the basic factors, namely that there has to be one year's residence in Canada before a man may qualify for war veterans allowance.
However, there are now a number of cases of servicemen who have stayed abroad, particularly in the United Kingdom. I know some administrative difficulty may be caused in respect of the Canadian servicemen who have lived entirely in the United States, and this has perhaps posed most of the problem on the negative side of this question.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
With regard to those who live in the United Kingdom, frankly I fail to see why, having amended our war veterans allowance provisions in the past few years, first of all the allowance should be payable to a recipient anywhere in the world, and second, that allied servicemen who have completed, either themselves or through their
DEBATES	2973
War Veterans Allowance Act widows in appropriate cases, ten years residence in Canada can qualify for war veterans allowance or whatever consequential allowances are payable under the Act, yet Canadian servicemen, and there are a large number of them, who have remained in the United Kingdom and married there, not having come back to Canada, are just as much servicemen as those who live in Canada. We have accepted the principle of paying benefits offshore. Therefore in those circumstances I am wondering why we disqualify so many by insisting on one year's residence in Canada.
A man who otherwise qualifies for war veterans allowance is obviously precluded for economic reasons from coming back to Canada and establishing one year's residence and then returning to the United Kingdom. You might as well ask him to walk to the moon. Yet why cannot this be done in these cases? I put this before the Minister so that he and the senior officials of the War Veterans Allowance Board can consider this point, which I think should be discussed the next time the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs meets.
I have a very urgent plea on behalf of these veterans, particularly those who live in the United Kingdom and Europe. Those who are closer on the continent of North America I have less sympathy for, although there may be some cases of hardship involving health. Nevertheless I have less sympathy for men on the North American continent who cannot establish a year's residence in Canada. But I do not think we can fault the man who is overseas. If we accept the principle of payments offshore, why cannot we remove this disqualifying bar from these veterans?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be those of commendation of the staff responsible for the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. We receive complaints from time to time from all kinds of people, but I remember the words of a former Minister of Veterans Affairs who said that a mistake of the mind will not be forgiven, but that he would forgive a mistake of the heart. I gave this bill some study over the week end and I commend the director of the Veterans' Land Act and his staff for accomplishing in this bill many of the things for which both the veterans and the staff had asked for. [DOT] (8:50 p.m.)

These amendments are generally speaking those sought by veterans and hon. Members of this place. Some may say that the requirement of $2,600 as the maximum advance on $18,000 is a little high, but I do not think too many people would object to it. We are encouraged by the proposal and will make

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUTHORITY OF DIRECTOR, HOME CONSTRUCTION ASSISTANCE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Members of this party support the principle and purpose of this bill and realize that a number of the suggested amendments have been suggested to the Cabinet by veterans organizations and to Members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, and that other amendments are the result of experience gained by officials administering the Act to date.
There has been a great amount of improvement in this type of legislation since the Soldier Settlement Act adopted after the first world war and the Canadian Farm Loans Act which followed that. I remember being a member of the Great War Veterans Association committee, which made recommendations for the amendment of the Soldier Settlement Act years ago, and later as a member of the Legion committee which made proposals which led to the adoption of what we now call the Veterans' Land Act.
I was also a member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs in 1945 when this legislation was first presented and know that it was drawn largely on the basis of experience of officials of the Soldier Settlement Board and the Canadian Farm Loans Act, as well as on the basis of the experience of the veterans themselves as represented by resolutions and briefs presented by veterans organizations.
It is quite true to say that this Veterans' Land Act legislation has been successful throughout the years, and I think it has been successful because of the fact that there has been co-operation between governments of the day, veterans organizations and officials, and veterans directly concerned. A great deal of credit is due Brigadier Rutherford, who was the former head of that Board, and who laid the foundation for supervision of farm credit in Canada. This principle was later adopted by the Farm Credit Corporation.
In that connection I should like to quote briefly from the Family Herald. This is not a magazine that is read by intellectuals, but generally by the farming population of Canada. Its editor, Mr. Cram, is interested in this legislation and generally in all aspects of farm legislation. This is what he had to say recently:
There are no statistics to show how many farmers there are in Canada today whose hopes of land ownership had been blighted by the depression of the thirties, then sidetracked by their
Veterans' Land Act
service in World War II, finally to see those hopes come to fruition under VLA loans. Their numbers are undoubtedly legion.
Apart from the provision of those individual opportunities the legacy which VLA leaves to Canadian agriculture will be a quarter century of practical, pragmatic administration of farm credit problems. Guided by some of the mistakes and misfortunes of its post-World War I predecessor, the Soldier Settlement Board, VLA was able to develop a program of assistance better tailored to the individual veterans capabilities and requirements.
On at least three major counts, VLA deserves special commendation. First, its program possessed the needed flexibility to develop with the changing tempo of Canadian farming. The somewhat modest loan limits established in the immediate post-war years were gradually extended as modern agricultural techniques began to demand larger and larger amounts of capital.
That is what this bill recognizes.
Second, from its very inception to the present time, VLA gave recognition to the needs of those veterans whose needs were so difficult to categorize: the smallholder, the part time farmer.
I am very glad to see that this is recognized because I have always maintained that there is a great place for smallholders and part-time farmers in this country. Many of these people supplement their income in this way. Very often they operate recreational facilities, such as small hotels or tourist accommodation resorts. For that reason I am pleased by this provision.
At no time in its history was VLA unduly swayed by economic planning which overlooked individual hopes or ambitions. Indeed, roughly half of the loans approved were for smallholders. In so doing, VLA recognized part-time farming as an economic fact and as a way of life which many veterans wanted and were capable of achieving.
There is no doubt about it. The annual reports of the Department show that they have been most successful in this respect.
Finally, years before anyone dreamed up the term, "supervised credit" VLA fieldmen were offering guidance and management advice to farming veterans. It was an approach which reflected the philosophy of VLA director Tom Rutherford and fortunately it followed him to the more liberally endowed Farm Credit Corporation.

I am pleased to answer your letter of the 10th June addressed to Mr. H. H. Milbum of the Taxation Division. You attached a copy of the letter addressed to you by Mr. Chris Spicer of Nakusp, B.C.
Mr. Spicer is concerned that the compensation received by persons who will be displaced by the construction of the High Arrow Dam from the B.C. Hydro and Power Authority may be subject to income tax.
In the usual course, it is quite certain that the assessors from the Taxation Division will have regard to these compensation payments to ensure that any resulting tax is paid as required by the statute. The statute is complex and its application may vary depending on the particular circumstances of the taxpayer, the nature of the property and of its use by such taxpayer, and the basis on which the actual compensation has been determined. For instance, it will make a difference whether the property was held to produce income
June 28, 1985

from a business, to produce rental income, as stock-in-trade, or solely for personal use.
In such circumstances, it is risky to generalize but it may be helpful to have the following general comments which would be applicable when a person receives compensation for property taken by expropriation:
1.	the compensation will be regarded as being for the physical assets expropriated even though consideration was given to intangibles, loss of income, etc., in arriving at the final compensation figure;
2.	where the physical assets include depreciable property a reasonable portion of the compensation will be considered as proceeds of disposition of such depreciable property and, in some cases, will result in recapture of all or part of the capital cost allowance previously claimed on such depreciable property;
3.	where the physical assets include stock-intrade (such as land of a dealer in real estate) a reasonable part of the compensation that would relate to such stock in trade would be included in income, and
4.	in some cases an amount will be paid in addition to the compensation to cover interest from the date the compensation is determined to the payment date. Such interest, when received, would be income subject to tax.
I am sorry that I cannot be more explicit but the provisions of the Income Tax Act cover such a variety of circumstances that almost every case must be considered on its own merit.
Yours truly,

Minister of National Revenue.

postpone these repayments during a particularly hard year it will save the farm unit, save the veteran from disaster, and maintain the value of the farm unit because an experienced man will be continuing its operation. maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-JOHN DARRELL PETERS-ALLEGED UNFAIRNESS IN SENTENCE
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-JOHN DARRELL PETERS-ALLEGED UNFAIRNESS IN SENTENCE
speechtext:
After all those moans and groans, I merely want to take up the case of a poor individual who is spending 20 years of his life in the penitentiary, and I think unjustly so. The other day I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) to look into the case of one John Darrell Peters, an inmate of a B.C. penitentiary, with respect to seeing whether or not he could order a new trial. The answer I got from the Minister was that a former Minister, Hon. Mr. Fulton, had reviewed the case quite thoroughly and come to the conclusion that there was no chance of a retrial and that the present Minister agreed with that decision. a sort of Fulton-Favreau formula in miniature.
Now, Mr. Peters has not been a model inmate in a penitentiary, I will admit that, from the outset. By "model" I mean he has not been docile or malleable to the rules inside the penitentiary. I submit that part of the reason for his attitude toward officialdom within the prison has been the treatment he received at the hands of the court and at the hands of the lawyer he retained. He was tried by one Magistrate Thoburn and sentenced to 20 years for a variety of offences. Mr. Peters has sworn a number of affidavits,
DEBATES	2985
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion which I hope I will have time to read into the record in order to put his case from his point of view. In one of those sworn on June 17, 1965 he says, and I quote:
That I, in fact, asked Magistrate Thoburn for a remand to "obtain and instruct counsel", and was refused,
That the hearing before Magistrate Thoburn was, to my knowledge, a session of "closed court",
That I was in a state of shock, and did not understand the import of the proceedings before Magistrate Thoburn,
That Magistrate Thoburn did not in any manner instruct me as to my right to obtain counsel, nor the seriousness of the said charges; and never advised me in any manner whatsoever,
That I was held without the benefit of help or assistance in the entire time of the proceedings before Magistrate Thoburn; and was in fact denied the one phone call, as prescribed by law; and was hindered and restrained from contacting help or assistance in all respects.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I do not want to take the time to read all the affidavit but just the salient parts from it. He says in another affidavit:
That in a letter, to C. B. Saunders, Esq. (Assistant Registrar, Supreme Court of Ontario, Osgoode Hall, Toronto, Ontario), dated the 25th day of April; and signed C. A. Thoburn, Magistrate; in respect to the said application for appeal, he delivered, or caused to be delivered, the following information, which was false, and caused the informant to suffer a denial of justice, namely-
Both accused were asked if they had counsel, to which they replied, "... no...". They were then asked if they wished to proceed today or did they want to obtain counsel. Both said that they wanted to plead guilty "today"-to use their own expression, ",. .we'll go on today, we want to get it over with.. ."
That upon examination of the Official Court Transcripts, on page 7; the only question that had been put thus far was; Clerk of the Court: How do you elect to be tried, John Darrell Peters? The Accused Peters: By the Magistrate. Clerk of the Court: Peters, how do you plead to all charges? The Accused Peters: Guilty.
There is another matter, in that there was an arrangement between himself and the police officers to plead guilty to certain charges, wipe them off the books and get a light sentence. The affidavit further reads:
That in a letter dated October 23, 1963; To: Frank Howard, Esq., M.P. (House of Commons, Ottawa, Ontario). And signed by C. A. Thoburn, Q.C. Magistrate, said the following in part, namely- I always ask the following questions when a person is charged with a serious offence:
1.	Are you prepared to proceed with your trial?
2.	Do you wish an opportunity to retain counsel?
If they say "yes" to the first and "no" to the
second, I then have the man arraigned.
Then further Peters swears:
That upon examination of the Official Court Transcripts, not one word, as set out in (3) and (5) as stated above, appears anywhere in the transcripts.

Mr. John Darrell Peters in another affidavit claims and states:
That having filed the said form, he duly hired and paid a Toronto Barrister, and Attorney at Law, one Gary K. C. Braund, and paid the said Mr. Braund the sum of $200 to appear and argue the appeal, and to purchase the transcripts.
That in a letter dated the 15th of January, 1964, directed to Professor Stuart Ryan, from the Office of the Registrar of the Court of Appeal of the Province of Ontario; and signed by Mr. J. A. Preston (Assistant Registrar) he stated in part as follows,
There was no counsel on the argument of the matter; however, the application together with a report of His Worship Magistrate Thobum, was before the members of the Court of Appeal and was considered by them before this order was made on May 26th, 1960.
That after numerous complaints to Mr. Braund, on August 15th, 1960, a letter was received addressed to the Governor of the Kingston Penitentiary, that said in part the following:
I am enclosing in your safe-keeping a money order in the amount of $50 to be given to John Peters... and was signed by Gary Braund.
Then, after a lot of other correspondence he finally got the remaining $150 from this lawyer, Gary Braund. I merely place these small parts of the whole case on the record to plead with the Minister to look more thoroughly into this case and give John Darrell Peters the benefit of the doubt, and give him another trial because he obviously did not receive justice at the hands of Magistrate Thobum. He obviously was led astray by this lawyer, Gary Braund, who said he would represent him in court and in fact did not, and he had to go to great lengths in order to get his money back.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-JOHN DARRELL PETERS-ALLEGED UNFAIRNESS IN SENTENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the document the hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) read from sounds very much like, although it may not have been identical
DEBATES	June 28, 1965
to, an affidavit dated March 22, 1965 sworn by John Darrell Peters, and forwarded by himself to myself on that date for forwarding in due course to the Minister, so that the particular facts referred to by Mr. Peters in that affidavit would have been before the Minister most recently in his consideration of the case.
No one, Mr. Speaker, would claim that the proceedings in the courts of justice are infallible. They are like any other human endeavour; they are subject to great fallibility both as to errors of judgment and errors of fact. But I think it should be borne in mind that in so far as any case can be, the facts concerning the conviction of John Darrell Peters have been very thoroughly examined at various levels. There has been a series of applications by way of prerogative writ in this province and in British Columbia. There was the application before the Ontario Court of Appeal and there was an application for leave to appeal heard before five justices of the Supreme Court, an application which was dismissed. In addition, the former Minister of Justice, as I know personally from the volume of the files, had extensively examined the situation surrounding this case. The material referred to by the hon. Member was also received by me and was entered for consideration.
Subject to the fallibility which these proceedings inevitably risk, this particular situation has been given as full a hearing as possible. Reasonable men acting fairly have decided that no injustice was done and I therefore conclude that the suggestion that the Minister might act under section 596 either in respect of the direction of a new trial or of a hearing before the court of appeal would not be justified in the circumstances.
